theme: I cry aloud to God; then I remember
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 77. You have read this psalm twice before, in Unit 6 and in Unit 11. Read it a third time as a prayer for the exile, and notice the line about God’s footprints. This time hold it beside Ezekiel’s vision of the chariot throne you have just read.
settingTheScene: Psalm 77 is a psalm of Asaph. Earlier readings looked at it as a lesson in remembering, and as the lament of the northern kingdom. Now, in the exile, a third reading is possible. Ezekiel has just seen that God’s throne moves on wheels and is not tied to Jerusalem. The psalmist says God’s way was through the sea, and his footprints were unseen. God is at work even when we cannot trace him.
observation: “I cry aloud to God, aloud to God, and he will hear me” (v. 1).
“In the day of my trouble I seek the Lord; in the night my hand is stretched out without wearying” (v. 2).
“Selah” appears after verses 3, 9, and 15, three pauses (vv. 3, 9, 15).
“Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has he in anger shut up his compassion?” (v. 9).
“I will ponder all your work, and meditate on your mighty deeds” (v. 12).
“Your way, O God, is holy. What god is great like our God?” (v. 13).
“You are the God who works wonders; you have made known your might among the peoples” (v. 14).
“Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen” (v. 19).
interpretation:
The three Selahs mark three pauses in the psalm, and they trace a journey. The first, after verse 3, comes after the psalmist says that remembering God makes him groan. The second, after verse 9, follows the string of questions about God’s compassion. The third, after verse 15, comes after the declaration that God has redeemed his people. The psalm moves from groaning, to doubt, to testimony, and each pause gives time to think.

The center of the psalm is verse 13: “Your way, O God, is holy.” The Hebrew can also mean, “Your way is in the sanctuary.” Both are true. God’s way is holy, set apart and pure. And it is found in his presence, not in our understanding. When the psalmist cannot explain what God is doing, he does not deny his goodness. He says the way is holy. He may not see all of it, but he trusts it.

This fits what Ezekiel saw. The living creatures and wheels moved in every direction, full of eyes. God sees all. His movements are not random, even though they are beyond our grasp. When the exiles felt that God had lost control, Ezekiel showed them his throne in the midst of the storm.

The final image of the psalm is quiet. “Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters; yet your footprints were unseen.” God passed through the sea, but left no trace. And then the last line: “You led your people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.” The great Redeemer led through two ordinary men.

In the exile, God was still leading, through prophets like Ezekiel, through the hidden hand of providence, through the covenant he had promised not to forget. The footprints were unseen, but he was walking ahead.
connection: Romans 11:33 says, “How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!” Job 23:8-10 expresses the same hiddenness: “If I go forward, he is not there… but he knows the way that I take.” Isaiah 55:8-9 says that his thoughts are higher than ours. Luke 24:13-35 shows Jesus walking beside the disciples unrecognized on the road to Emmaus. Romans 8:28 says that God works all things together for good. John 13:7: “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.”
application:
Look back at a hard period and ask where God’s footprints might have been unseen at the time.

Trace one “pause” in your own faith: groaning, doubt, or testimony. Where are you now?

Pray “Your way, O God, is holy” as an act of trust in something you do not understand.
prayerPrompts: Cry aloud to God, and tell him what troubles you.
Remember his wonders and rest on them.
Praise him as the God who works wonders.
